blocks.text: She knew her grandmother, who lived in a neighbourhood where Spanish exiles had recreated their own little Spain. She felt immersed in that atmosphere. However, people spoke to her in French. She was there, and they were somewhere else. As a quiet child, people used to tell her: ‘Well then, have you lost your tongue ?’ She never learnt to speak Spanish. She first sought to fill these silences by meeting Spanish exiles in France, then by travelling the length and breadth of Aragon, the land her grandparents had left before their exile. But she could not find her place; the two territories, the two timeframes, remained divided. A turning point led her to her family’s archive photographs; she felt the need to plunge into the gap. It was by intervening on the very fabric of her images that she was able to reinterpret the world in which she grew up. She tore, erased, scraped, then re-glued, assembled, superimposed and transported to Spain these hybrid, hand-crafted photographic objects. She saw the void transform into flesh. This living material has brought depth to the anonymous part of her history. Removed from its intimate context, this work speaks to a collective memory, questions the effects of exile on subsequent generations and creates the framework for a transformation of the past into the present.
* (The title cannot be translated because the word enf(r)ance is a contraction of enfance (childhood) and France).
